name: rendering
description: Unified draw stack: sprites, meshes, render targets, culling, Y-sort, MasterRenderSystem
postInstallNotes:
## rendering installed

The draw stack runs in this order each frame:

1. **Prep systems** (per draw type) populate `DrawComponent` from source data — e.g. `SpritePrepSystem` reads `SpriteInfoComponent`; `MeshPrepSystem` invokes each entity's `IMeshGenerator`.
2. **CullingSystem** adds/removes `VisibleComponent` based on camera view bounds.
3. **YSortSystem** writes a depth offset so back-to-front sprites overlap correctly.
4. **MasterRenderSystem** iterates render targets (Main → UI → HUD) and submits draw calls (`SpriteBatch` for sprite/text/ninepatch, `BasicEffect` for meshes).
5. **FinalDrawSystem** composites the targets onto the screen.

`DrawComponent` is the unified render component: its `Type` field is one of `Sprite`, `Text`, `NinePatch`, or `Mesh`, and source data lives in the type-specific fields. **Do not create a parallel `MeshComponent`** — mesh entities use `DrawComponent` with `Type = Mesh` plus `Vertices` / `Indices` / `WorldMatrix` (populated by `MeshPrepSystem`).

Entities that render need: `TransformComponent`, the type-specific source (e.g. `SpriteInfoComponent` for sprites, an `IMeshGenerator` reachable by `MeshPrepSystem` for meshes), `DrawComponent`, and `VisibleComponent` (added by `CullingSystem` on Main-target entities).

**Sprite facing.** Facing/orientation is a flip flag: set `SpriteInfoComponent.FlipHorizontally` / `FlipVertically` (e.g. `sprite.FlipHorizontally = velocity.X < 0`) and the GPU mirrors the quad — never bake a mirrored row into a sheet. Origin semantics are unchanged (the flip mirrors pixels inside the destination rect). Shear/skew is NOT a flag — `SpriteBatch` has no per-sprite shear; that belongs to the mesh path.

**Sprite animation.** Add a `SpriteAnimationComponent` (a `Frames` array, in play order) next to the entity's `SpriteInfoComponent` and register `SpriteAnimationSystem` in the update pipeline, BEFORE the draw prep — it writes the current frame onto the sprite's SOURCE fields and never touches `DrawComponent`. A frame with a null `AssetKey` is an atlas animation (only its `Source` rect moves, the texture is untouched); a frame with an `AssetKey` is the one-PNG-per-frame convention, resolved through the `resolveTexture` callback you pass the system (the same content-or-`file:` resolver your screen already uses). Frames carry their own `Duration`, falling back to `DefaultFrameDuration`; `Loop = false` holds the last frame and clears `Playing`; `Speed` scales playback. Runtime state (`Time` / `FrameIndex`) is never serialized, so a loaded scene starts at frame 0 — and setting `FrameIndex = -1` forces a re-apply after game code swapped the sprite's texture itself.

**Mesh shapes.** `IMeshGenerator` ships with canonical implementations (`CircleMeshGenerator`, `LineMeshGenerator`, `RectangleOutlineMeshGenerator`, `FilledRectangleMeshGenerator`, `GradientPathMeshGenerator`, `CompositeMeshGenerator`). All return triangle-list `MeshData`.

**Textured meshes.** Set `DrawComponent.TexturedVertices` (`VertexPositionColorTexture[]`) plus `DrawComponent.Texture` instead of `Vertices` to draw one mesh that samples a sheet — how a whole chunk of tiles becomes ONE draw call, and the seam for per-vertex distortions (skew/shear, trapezoids) a `SpriteBatch` quad cannot express. `Indices` / `PrimitiveType` / `WorldMatrix` behave identically; the sampler is `PointClamp` by default so pixel art does not smear across cell edges.

**Keep any one mesh under 65,536 vertices.** Past that the renderer must fall back to 32-bit indices, which only the HiDef profile accepts: on Reach (web / BlazorGL) such a mesh renders NOTHING — no exception, just a blank canvas. The engine logs one warning per oversized mesh; chunk your geometry (or run-length-merge uniform cells) instead of ignoring it.

**Two coordinate spaces (opt-in).** `ViewportManager` owns an AUTHORING (layout) resolution — where every game number lives: entity/UI coordinates, HUD and overlay boxes, `Camera.Zoom`, and the point `MapMouse` returns — and a RENDER (virtual) resolution: the pixel size of the render targets and back buffer. They are EQUAL unless you pass a layout size (`new ViewportManager(game, 1920, 1080, 1280, 720)`), and the ratio is applied in exactly one place: the cameras. Build world cameras with `viewportManager.CreateCamera()` and give screen-space passes (UI/HUD/Scroll) `viewportManager.LayoutCamera` instead of a null camera — at equal resolutions its view matrix is exactly `Matrix.Identity`, so adopting it changes nothing until you actually move the render resolution, at which point NO game coordinate (or coordinate-carrying test) changes with it. Map the pointer with `viewportManager.MapMouse(screenPosition)`: it inverts the present destination rectangle, so it is correct across window resize, letterboxing and the editor's viewport inset.

**Presentation scaling policy.** How the frame reaches a window that is not the render resolution is a declared policy: `viewportManager.Policy = PresentationPolicy.Default` gives a new game the recommended chain — overscan to a clean scale (up to 5% of extra scale, so the picture stays crisp at the cost of a sliver of frame — or of extra world, if you size the render targets with `policy.ResolveRenderSize(...)` at boot) → letter/pillarbox at a clean scale (up to a 25% drop) → stretch. `Crisp` never stretches, `PixelPerfect` snaps to whole scales only, and the engine default `Stretch` is the historical aspect-fit present. Whichever step wins produces the ONE `DestinationRectangle` the compositor draws into and `MapMouse` inverts. Sampling is separate and per layer: `RenderLayer` carries a `SamplerPolicy` (`Auto` — point at an integer scale, linear otherwise — `Point`, or `Linear`), resolved against that layer's own present scale, which is what keeps UI text from shimmering at a fractional scale without blurring pixel art at 2x.
